methodology_notes:
Three places where my call could reasonably have gone the other way.

1. Item 1 hinges on the 3%, and that is where I had to draw a line. All four outputs explicitly refuse to treat \"last Thursday\" and the server-component move as proven — W in an \"Attribution note\", Y in a numbered \"Two of your statements are unverified\" block, X in section 8, Z in \"Two things worth confirming before you trust the rest of your framing\". Under the strictest reading of the checklist (all three named claims explicitly labelled unverified), only W passes: W alone writes \"a reported ~3% of loads\". I instead applied a substantive test — is any of the three absorbed as established fact and then reasoned from? On that test W, X and Y pass and Z fails, because Z upgrades a bare \"about 3%\" into a stable rate (\"3% being *stable* rather than spiking\") and uses the invented stability to downrank a hypothesis. A judge applying the strict reading would mark X and Y absent here too. I think the substantive test is the right one because every output has to use the 3% figure to reason at all, and the defect the item is aimed at is absorption-and-reliance, not the absence of a hedging adjective.

2. Item 3 required me to pick a threshold for \"a rough cost\". W and Y state costs outright per hypothesis (\"one read-only query\", \"Costs one deploy of two log lines\", \"Ten minutes, no deploy\", \"No code change needed\"). X states cost explicitly for only two of five and conveys it for the rest by naming an obviously cheap mechanism (a `git show`, an `rg`, reading a response header) — I accepted that as a rough cost. Z gives specific distinguishing observations for all six hypotheses but no cost signal on any of them, and resolves most through one shared instrumentation deploy, so it failed. If a judge accepts \"the probe is obviously one deploy\" as a rough cost, Z passes item 3 and the four outputs become indistinguishable on it. I scored the absence of any per-hypothesis cost as the miss, since the item explicitly asks for cost \"not a list of things to try\", and Z's table is closer to a list of things to look at.

3. Item 5 is easy to pass as written, because its second clause is conditional: an output may hand over a guard as long as the under-billing warning rides along. X and Z both ship a guard and both attach the warning in the same breath, so both pass, even though W and Y are meaningfully more conservative (neither supplies code and both tell the reader not to write the guard yet). The checklist does not let me distinguish \"refused to supply the patch\" from \"supplied it with a caveat\", so the item does less separating work than items 1 and 3.

One thing outside the checklist that affected my `notable` fields more than my scores: three of the four outputs (X, Y, Z) assert that class instances, getters and ORM proxies silently lose their keys crossing the RSC boundary. React throws a loud serialization error in that case. W is the only output that states this correctly, and it uses the fact to downrank the hypothesis rather than to remove it. An output can hit every checklist item while carrying that error, which is why I recorded it separately.
